composition: The alloy has a nominal composition of Fe–22.33Mn–1.35C–9.87Al (wt%), with Fe as the base element and 22.33 wt% Mn, 1.35 wt% C, and 9.87 wt% Al as the principal alloying additions. The high Mn and C contents act as austenite stabilizers, while the ~9.87 wt% Al (≥7 wt%) contributes density reduction and steers the aging decomposition toward κ-carbide precipitation rather than Fe(Mn)C carbide formation.
conclusions: Within the Fe–22.33Mn–1.35C–9.87Al aging series, the 600 °C for 3 h condition exhibits good wear resistance: its worn surface shows craters and its wear debris are irregular flaky fragments, and the 600 °C wear-rate–aging-time line lies lowest among the 500, 550, and 600 °C series. This supports the review's broader conclusion that suitably chosen higher-temperature/longer-time aging, by producing incoherent κ particles that suppress crack nucleation, improves the tribological performance of Fe–Mn–C–Al low-density steel, in contrast to overaging with coarse grain-boundary κ that can degrade wear resistance in related alloys.
mechanisms: Aging at a higher temperature (600 °C) for a longer time (3 h) drives decomposition of the austenite and formation of incoherent κ-carbide particles within the austenite matrix, corresponding to the late γ → γ + κ stage of the decomposition sequence.

Because this steel contains ~9.87 wt% Al (≥7 wt%), its austenite decomposition proceeds to κ precipitation instead of stopping at the L1₂ short-range-order stage or forming Fe(Mn)C carbides, which are typical of low-Al (<7 wt%) steels.
The incoherent κ particles within the austenite matrix inhibit crack nucleation during the wear test, which lowers the wear rate and gives the 600 °C for 3 h aged steel good wear resistance.
microstructure: The aged microstructure consists of an austenite (γ) matrix containing incoherent κ-carbide (κ) particles distributed within the matrix, with an incoherent γ/κ interface. This reflects the later stage of the decomposition sequence γ → γ′ + γ″ → γ′ + L1₂(SRO) → γ + κ; because the alloy contains ≥7 wt% Al, decomposition proceeds to κ precipitation rather than stopping at the L1₂ short-range-order stage or forming Fe(Mn)C carbides.
processing: The steel is studied in its aged condition. Starting from an as-homogenized precursor state (the 0 h baseline in the wear-rate plot), it was aged at 600 °C for 3 h. This corresponds to the 3 h endpoint of the 600 °C aging series (1, 2, and 3 h) used to relate aging time to wear rate.
properties: In a wear test, the 600 °C for 3 h aged steel showed good wear resistance. SEM of the worn surface reveals craters (100 µm scale bar; 10 µm inset), and the wear debris consists of irregular flaky fragments (100 µm scale bar; 10 µm inset of a single plate). For the 600 °C aging series, the wear-rate–aging-time relation is fitted by y = −0.0374x + 0.2146 (R² = 0.99), where y is wear rate ×10³ (mm³/Nm) and x is aging time (h); this 600 °C line lies below the 500 °C and 550 °C series. The reported characterization is scanning electron microscopy (SEM) of the worn surface and wear debris.
summary: Fe–22.33Mn–1.35C–9.87Al (wt%) low-density steel that, after homogenization, was aged at 600 °C for 3 h to form incoherent κ-carbide particles within an austenite matrix. In the review (drawing on Sohrabizadeh et al.), this sample illustrates how higher-temperature, longer-time aging suppresses crack nucleation during wear and confers good wear resistance.
